newsitem.title: USA: Hurricanes claim heavy toll in 1996 season.
newsitem.headline: Hurricanes claim heavy toll in 1996 season.

text.p: Hurricanes wrought death and destruction from the islands of the Caribbean to the United States' Atlantic seaboard in an unexpectedly intense season which ends, officially at least, on Saturday.

Homes and lives were ruined from the poor barrios of Havana to luxury beach houses on the southeast U.S. coast. During Hurricane Fran, workers sandbagged streets near the White House in Washington to hold back flooding.
People saw their livelihoods washed away as floods doused tobacco fields in Virginia and the Carolinas, banana groves in the West Indies, and sugar plantations in Cuba and the Dominican Republic.
Hurricane Lili also provoked a political storm as a furious debate erupted in Miami over whether to send relief aid to communist Cuba.

"The 1996 hurricane season was characterised by very high hurricane activity ... 1996 was a special year," the Colorado State University's Department of Atmospheric Science, a renowned hurricane watching centre, said in its annual report.
It listed 13 named storms, nine of them hurricanes, over a total of 45 days from June 1 through to the end of November.

During an average season there are 10 weather systems that become tropical storms, of which six mature into hurricanes. Many forecasters believe the last two seasons are marking the beginning of a cycle of increased storm activity. In 1995 there were 19 tropical storms, of which 11 became hurricanes.

This year storms followed in quick succession, sometimes walloping the same area twice as people struggled to recover. Wherever they hit there was a familiar litany of damage -- power lines tumbled, bridges crumbled, roads flooded and houses swept away.
"This is a year we'll remember for a long, long time," Tom Hegley of the North Carolina Emergency Management Centre said.

One of the season's most dramatic moments was captured on film during Hurricane Hortense as Miguel Ariel Rodriguez and Jose Luis de Leon hung on grimly to ropes across a raging torrent in Puerto Rico to bring a baby to safety.
Five members of the family were rescued from their washed-away house but six were killed.
Hortense killed at least 22 people when it drenched Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic in September. Swollen rivers burst their banks and deadly mudslides rushed down slopes.
In the United States, Hurricane Fran will be remembered as one of the most ferocious to whack the southeast.

Hitting land in September at aptly named Cape Fear, North Carolina, and tearing up the coast, it took the lives of at least 34 Americans. Some were swept away in cars and two were trapped by rising floodwaters in the basement of their Philadelphia home.
Governor Jim Hunt told President Bill Clinton when he visited North Carolina in the aftermath of the storm that it was the worst disaster the state had ever suffered.
"The only ggod thing about Fran is that everyone's stopped talklng about Hazel (in 1954)," Hegley said Wednesday.

"We still have a lot of people trying to get back on their feet. A lot of people still aren't back in their homes. What we're hearing from building contractors is some repairs could take a year to get done."

Losses in agriculture from Fran were estimated at $616 million, with tobacco bearing the brunt. Damage to unharvested tobacco crops in some parts of North and South Carolina and Virgina was total, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said.

The insurance trade industry group Property Claim Services estimated insured property damage from Fran at $1.6 billion and from the earlier Hurricane Bertha at $135 million. It put damage in Puerto Rico from Hortense at $150 million.
Hurricane Lili hit Cuba with full force in October and started a storm of a different kind in Miami.
It left thousands of people homeless and caused extensive crop damage, prompting Miami's Cuban exile community to mobilise to collect and ship down relief supplies.

Right-wingers objected to the humanitarian operation, saying it would benefit President Fidel Castro. When the aid arrived the Cuban government rejected hundreds of boxes and cans which the exiles had marked with political slogans.
Storm-related deaths during the season were reported from Nicaragua and Honduras in Central America to the other side of the Atlantic in Britain, where Lili's remnants pitched up.
With the season now closing in, the resort town of Topsail Island, North Carolina, was looking forward.
"There's no question in our mind we'll be ready for tourists by Easter," said town manager Eric Peterson.
On Sept. 5, a 12-foot (four-metre) surge from Hurricane Fran swept three to five feet (1-1.5 metre) of sand onto the town.
Soldiers have cleared most of the debris but a dislocated house still sits in a marsh outside Peterson's office.
"That's on my to-do list," he said.
